title: The Pink
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a queen to whom God had given no children. Every morning she went out into the garden and prayed to God in heaven to grant her a son or a daughter. One day an angel came down from heaven and said to her, “Be at peace. You will have a son who has the power of wishing, so that whatever he wishes for in the world, he will have.” She went to the king and told him the joyful news, and when the time came she gave birth to a son, and the king was filled with happiness.

Every morning she took the child with her to the garden where the wild animals were kept, and washed in a clear stream there. One day, when the child was a little older, it was lying in her arms and she fell asleep. The old cook, who knew the child had the power of wishing, came and stole it away. He killed a hen, cut it into pieces, and dripped some of its blood on the queen’s apron and dress. Then he carried the child off to a secret place, where a nurse was forced to nurse it, and ran to the king and accused the queen of letting wild animals take her child from her. When the king saw the blood on her apron, he believed it. He flew into such a rage that he ordered a high tower to be built, with no way for the sun or moon to shine in, and had his wife shut up inside and walled in. She was to stay there for seven years without food or drink, and starve to death. But God sent two angels from heaven in the shape of white doves, and they flew to her twice a day and brought her food until the seven years were over.

The cook, though, thought to himself, “If the child has the power of wishing and I stay here, he could easily bring trouble down on me.” So he left the palace and went to the boy, who was by now old enough to talk, and said to him, “Wish for a beautiful palace for yourself, with a garden and everything that goes with it.” The words were barely out of the boy’s mouth when everything he had wished for was there. After a while the cook said to him, “It isn’t good for you to be so alone. Wish for a pretty girl to keep you company.” So the king’s son wished for one, and she stood before him at once, more beautiful than any painter could have painted her. The two of them played together and loved each other with all their hearts, while the old cook went hunting like a nobleman. But then it occurred to him that the king’s son might one day wish to be with his father, and that this would put him in great danger. So he went out, took the girl aside, and said, “Tonight, when the boy is asleep, go to his bed and drive this knife into his heart. Bring me his heart and his tongue. If you don’t do it, you will lose your life.” Then he left, and when he came back the next day she had not done it. She said, “Why should I shed the blood of an innocent boy who has never harmed anyone?” The cook said again, “If you don’t do it, it will cost you your own life.” After he had gone, she had a young hind brought to her and ordered it killed. She took its heart and tongue and laid them on a plate, and when she saw the old man coming, she said to the boy, “Lie down in your bed and pull the covers over you.” Then the wicked man came in and said, “Where are the boy’s heart and tongue?” The girl handed him the plate, but the king’s son threw off the quilt and said, “You old sinner, why did you want to kill me? Now I pronounce your sentence. You will become a black poodle with a gold collar around your neck, and you will eat burning coals until flames burst from your throat.” As soon as he had spoken these words, the old man was turned into a poodle with a gold collar around his neck, and the cooks were told to bring live coals, and he ate them until flames shot out of his throat. The king’s son stayed there a little while longer, thinking of his mother and wondering whether she was still alive. At last he said to the girl, “I want to go home to my own country. If you come with me, I will look after you.” “Oh,” she answered, “it is such a long way, and what would I do in a strange land where nobody knows me?” She did not seem quite willing, and since they could not bear to be parted, he wished her into a beautiful pink and took her with him. Then he set off for his own country, with the poodle running behind him. He went to the tower where his mother was shut up, and since it was so high, he wished for a ladder that would reach all the way to the top. He climbed up, looked inside, and called, “Dearest mother, Lady Queen, are you still alive, or are you dead?” She answered, “I have just eaten, and I am still full,” for she thought the angels were there. He said, “I am your dear son, the one the wild animals were said to have torn from your arms. But I am still alive, and I will soon set you free.” Then he climbed down again, went to his father, and had himself announced as a stranger and a huntsman, and asked whether the king could use his services. The king said yes: if he was skillful and could bring in game, he could come into his service, but there had never been any deer in that district or anywhere in the country. The huntsman promised to supply as much game as the royal table could possibly use. He called all the huntsmen together and told them to come out into the forest with him. There he had them form a great circle, open at one end, and he stood in the opening and began to wish. More than two hundred deer came running into the circle at once, and the huntsmen shot them. They were loaded onto sixty country carts and driven home to the king, and for once he could load his table with game, after years without any.

The king was very pleased, and ordered his whole household to dine with him the next day, and held a great feast. When everyone had gathered, he said to the huntsman, “Since you are so clever, you will sit beside me.” The huntsman replied, “Lord King, Your Majesty must excuse me. I am only a poor huntsman.” But the king insisted, saying, “You will sit beside me,” until he did. As he sat there, he thought of his dearest mother, and wished that one of the king’s chief servants would speak of her and ask how the queen was doing in the tower, and whether she was still alive or had died. He had hardly made the wish when the marshal began, “Your Majesty, we live in joy here, but how does the queen fare in the tower? Is she still alive, or has she died?” But the king answered, “She let my dear son be torn to pieces by wild animals. I will not have her named.” Then the huntsman stood up and said, “Gracious lord father, she is still alive, and I am her son. I was not carried off by wild animals. It was that wretch, the old cook, who tore me from her arms while she slept and smeared her apron with the blood of a chicken.” Then he took the dog with the golden collar and said, “There is the wretch!” He had live coals brought, and the dog was forced to swallow them in front of everyone, until flames burst from its throat. The huntsman then asked the king whether he would like to see the dog in its true shape, and wished him back into the cook, who stood there at once in his white apron with his knife at his side. When the king saw him, he flew into a rage and ordered him thrown into the deepest dungeon. Then the huntsman went on, “Father, would you like to see the girl who raised me so tenderly, and who was later supposed to murder me, but did not, though her own life depended on it?” The king answered, “Yes, I would like to see her.” The son said, “Most gracious father, I will show her to you as a beautiful flower.” He put his hand in his pocket, took out the pink, and set it on the royal table, and it was so beautiful that the king had never seen one to match it. Then the son said, “Now I will show her to you in her own form,” and he wished her into a girl again, and she stood there, so beautiful that no painter could have made her more so.

The king sent two maids and two attendants to the tower to fetch the queen and bring her to the royal table. But when she was led in, she ate nothing. She said, “The gracious and merciful God who kept me alive in the tower will soon set me free.” She lived three days longer and then died a happy death. When she was buried, the two white doves that had brought her food in the tower, and were angels from heaven, followed her body and settled on her grave. The old king ordered the cook torn into four pieces, but grief ate away at the king’s own heart, and he soon died. His son married the beautiful girl he had carried with him as a flower in his pocket, and whether they are still alive or not, God knows.
